item.title: Heartbroken fathers find divine hope in secret notes left by girls killed in Camp Mystic flood
item.description: Fathers of Camp Mystic flash flood victims share how secret journals filled with Bible verses and deep faith bring comfort to their grieving families.
item.content:encoded:
One year after flash flooding at Camp Mystic took 28 lives, three fathers are sharing how their young daughters’ private faith continues to lift their families.

Speaking on "Saturday in America," Ryan DeWitt, Wade Lytal and Cole Naylor shared how their daughters' deep-rooted faith has sustained them through tragedy. DeWitt and Lytal said they found journals their daughters left behind filled with Bible verses, prayers and messages to God, bringing them comfort as they grieved.

"We knew that she was deeply rooted in her faith, but she wasn't outward about it or braggadocious about it. She just felt it. She felt very deeply," Ryan DeWitt said of his daughter Molly, who was 9 years old when she died in the floods.

"She just had the biggest heart, and we taught her as much as we could, but there was certainly something else at play, and that was her faith, and it was comforting. As difficult as those days were and still are, it's comforting to know how close she was to God," he added.

DEVASTATED MOTHER BLAMES SOFT-ON-CRIME POLICIES AFTER CAREER CRIMINAL IS CHARGED IN SON’S DEATH

The fathers each recalled moments when they learned more about the depth of their daughters’ faith. DeWitt shared that Molly kept notebooks under her bed filled with hand-drawn crosses and Bible verses, including one page that read, "I can do anything through Christ."

Wade Lytal recalled entering the bedroom of his 8-year-old daughter, Kellyanne, weeks after the tragedy and pulling open a drawer to find a journal entry that read, "Jesus I love you. Thank you for dying on the cross for all of our sins."

"I think that's the most important responsibility that we have as parents is making sure that, you know, our children are raised to love the Lord," Lytal said.

YOUNG TEXAS CAMP SURVIVOR DESCRIBES HARROWING MOMENT SHE PREPARED FOR WORST DURING DEADLY FLOOD

Lytal said that after the flood, he no longer believes in coincidences and views finding her journal as a gift during a dark time.

"We were going through her things and the first drawer I pulled open, that was the notebook that was in there. We saw what she wrote, and it did bring some comfort to us in a very, very dark moment in our life," he said.

Cole Naylor, father of 8-year-old Wynne, emphasized that reliance on daily prayer has carried his family through the loss. He shared that he refuses to speak about his daughter in the past tense, standing firm in the promise that they will be reunited.

"Our girls are very much alive," Naylor said. "They are more alive than any one of us are. Alive in heaven, we don't get to see them, we don't get to touch them, we don’t get to kiss them anymore, but they're with us, and we will see them again."

CAMP MYSTIC PULLS PLAN TO REOPEN THIS SUMMER AFTER BACKLASH FROM GRIEVING FAMILIES

In April, Camp Mystic announced it would not be reopening for the 2026 season despite having previously planned to welcome hundreds of girls back to the property.

"No administrative process or summer season should move forward while families continue to grieve," the camp said in a statement.

"This decision is intended to remove any doubt that Camp Mystic has heard the concerns expressed by grieving families, members of the Texas House and Senate investigating committees and citizens across our state. Respect for those voices requires that we step back now."

item.title: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sends trans inclusion memo after Enes Freedom, Royce White announcements
item.description: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert addressed teams in a memo as Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White each declared for the 2027 WNBA Draft.
item.content:encoded:
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent a letter to teams on Friday addressing concerns over the inclusion of transgender athletes in the league as two former NBA players announced their intentions to declare for the next WNBA Draft.

"I know many of you have received questions in recent weeks regarding transgender athlete participation in women’s basketball, and I expect this topic will continue to receive significant attention," Engelbert wrote in the memo, per The Associated Press.

"I wanted to reach out to share how we are approaching these conversations at the league office and to thank those of you who have responded to questions from the media with thoughtfulness and professionalism."

THE WNBA HAS LIMITED OPTIONS AFTER TWO MEN DECLARED FOR THE DRAFT, AND THOSE OPTIONS AREN'T GREAT

Engelbert went on to call the debate "nuanced."

"We recognize that this is a complex and nuanced topic, and we will continue to have important conversations with all of you and the Players Association in the weeks and months ahead," Engelbert said in the memo. "We also plan to convene additional discussions and offer listening sessions for any team leaders who would like to participate. Your perspectives and feedback are invaluable, and I appreciate those who have already reached out to share their thoughts."

Engelbert's memo came on the same day that two former NBA pros, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, said they plan to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft. The announcements became the top trending topic across social media, as sports fans across the world mocked the WNBA for its policy that doesn't clearly define who is allowed to play in the league based on genetic sex.

The WNBA players’ association also released a statement on social media Friday that emphasized diversity and inclusion while saying the group "will not be used as political pawns."

WNBPA ISSUES STATEMENT EMBRACING DIVERSITY AND INCLUSION AMID TRANS ATHLETE DEBATE IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

"We embrace justice equity, diversity, and inclusion," the statement read. "Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women’s sports while creating transformational change. Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns."

The entire WNBA has become the epicenter for the national debate on trans athletes in women's sports in recent weeks after Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham, a fan favorite teammate of Caitlin Clark, revealed her stance supporting the protection of women's sports in an ESPN interview in July.

Since then, four head coaches have gone on record with responses to questions about the issues, with two of them, Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve and Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase, appearing to support the inclusion of trans athletes in women's sports.

Now, Kanter and White's entrance into the conversation has amplified the discussion across the sports realm, and it appears that Engelbert now has to address the issues.

item.title: Everyone wants what one minor league baseball team put out as a hilarious tribute to the Carolina Hurricanes
item.description: The Fayetteville Woodpeckers unveiled a Carolina Hurricanes tribute jersey that simply reads "PECKERS" across the front, and fans are loving it.
item.content:encoded:
I love minor league sports.

That's because, while at the top levels they're often worried about taking political stands to the point that the WNBA is like, "Meh, we're not going to slam the door on letting fellas play just yet," minor league teams have to focus on putting butts in seats. The best way to do that is with fun promotions.

So, that's what we're getting from one minor league ballclub's unintentionally — or, I think more likely, intentionally — hilarious tribute sweaters to the Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes.

The Fayetteville Woodpeckers — the Single-A affiliate of the Houston Astros — don't play too far from Raleigh, home of the Hurricanes. So, it makes sense that they would want to bathe in the warm glow of a Stanley Cup win.

And the best way to do that? This phenomenal jersey!

I know what it says.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Imagine wearing that jersey outside a 100-mile radius of Fayetteville. There's a good chance no one will have any clue why you own a hockey sweater that says "PECKERS" across the front.

And, frankly, I don't think it's anyone's business. You do you, pal.

I also get the feeling at least one kid will have to take a detour to the principal's office or flip their jersey inside-out in a couple of weeks when school gets underway. I promise you, some humorless school marm who only knows baseball from Ernest Lawrence Thayer's 1888 poem, "Casey at the Bat," won't get it (but will somehow still understand that "pecker" is a slang term for male genitalia).

But the public response has been about as good as the organization could hope for.

You rarely do anything on the internet that garners universal acclaim — trust me; I know — but I think the Peckers sweater may have done it.

Unfortunately, unless the plans change, only the first 1,350 fans at the Woodpeckers' game on August 15 will be able to cop them.

item.title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to what the Senate did and didn’t do overnight
item.description: Despite confirming Todd Blanche as Attorney General, the Senate wrapped its summer session with major legislative priorities unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
The Senate wrapped up its summer session at 4:57 a.m. ET.

Senators knocked two major items off their checklist. They confirmed Todd Blanche as the nation’s 88th Attorney General. 

They also approved a bipartisan interim spending bill that likely goes a long way toward preventing a government shutdown in October.

But nearly as important as what senators accomplished is what didn’t get done.

The Senate did not stay in session and attempt to pass the SAVE America Act. 

In fact, there was not even procedural stunting by the pro-SAVE America Act Republicans, who advocated blowing up the August recess.

TRUMP PUMPS BRAKES ON SENATE BUDGET PLAN, DELAYING GOP SAVE AMERICA PUSH

Moreover, the Senate did not take a vote on a budget framework which could enable them to eventually tack on some election integrity measures – and pass them at a later date in a bill not subject to a filibuster.

Expect some conservatives to rail against the Senate for not working this out. 

The SAVE America Act continues to lack votes. However, advocates of the bill can use the decision by the Senate to leave town without passing it as an opportunity to apply pressure on its opponents.

That said, the Senate did take a test vote on a more narrow voter ID bill backed by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. The Senate blocked that bill. 

But the test vote got Democrats on the record for opposing it. And giving Husted a vote on his measure was a tactical move to boost his chances in a competitive race this fall against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio.

The Senate did not take a test vote on the bipartisan bill to regulate money for intercollegiate athletics – despite the endorsement by the Big 10 and SEC. 

PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT STALLS IN OVERNIGHT SENATE SHOWDOWN, VOTE PUSHED TO SEPTEMBER AFTER CHAOTIC EVENING

In fact, President Trump even implored the Senate to stay in session in August to pass the bill authored by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Democrat on the panel. 

The legislation was beset by an internecine fight among Republicans about whether the legislation kept men from competing in women’s sports. 

The President published a full-throated endorsement of the legislation Friday night, declaring that the measure did go far enough. "Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying," wrote the President on Truth Social.

 In an overnight statement, Cruz said that the bill was still in play.

"The good news is that when the Senate returns in September, the Protect College Sports Act will be one of our first orders of business, having locked in a vote," said Cruz.

However, no vote is officially secured on the Senate docket.

But what about a test vote on a bill to regulate cryptocurrency?

It was thought that the Senate might pursue that bill in the closing days of the summer session. But the differences were just too wide to close. 

However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up a procedural vote on cryptocurrency for September 15.

item.title: University of Michigan plans to shield 2027 freshman letter grades from transcripts in new mental health plan
item.description: The University of Michigan's new pass-fail grading policy for 2027 freshmen aims to curb the mental health crisis, but a psychotherapist warns it may backfire.
item.content:encoded:
Freshmen at the University of Michigan next year are set to get a semester-long break from having letter grades appear on their transcripts, as school officials look for new ways to combat the "mental health crisis" affecting higher education.

Starting in fall 2027, incoming first-year students enrolled in the public research university's College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) will have their first-semester grades designated as pass or no credit on their transcripts in an attempt to "curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals," according to the university.

"Our goal is to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys — core elements of a liberal arts and sciences education," the statement continued.

EDUCATION SECRETARY LINDA MCMAHON RIPS CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE ‘COMPROMISE,’ TELLS NEWSOM TO ‘PICK A SIDE’

The LSA, which is the largest of the university’s 19 colleges and serves approximately 19,700 undergraduate students, will provide students with their letter grades throughout the semester — but will not include the final average on their transcripts.

Transcripts will instead show a "P" for pass or "NC" for no credit.

The covered grades will not be factored into students' grade point averages, a move university officials say will give first-year students greater freedom to explore academically.

"For example, they can explore a subject that may not come easily to them or take a course in a new field without the fear that a low grade may have long-term consequences," the university added. " LSA is investing in students’ well-being and growth by fostering a culture of connection and collaboration — rather than competition."

HARVARD FACULTY VOTE TO CAP 'A' GRADES AT 20% IN SWEEPING EFFORT TO COMBAT DECADES OF GRADE INFLATION

Under the new policy, university officials will keep students' first-semester letter grades internally for administrative purposes, including academic advising, potential academic awards and scholarships, internship and other professional applications, athletic eligibility, compliance reporting, degree progress and financial aid determinations.

Additionally, the 2027 policy only applies to incoming freshmen enrolled in the LSA, with school officials adding there is no opt-out option.

"An opt-in structure would defeat the purpose of facilitating students’ transition to campus, supporting mental health and well-being, and bolstering intrinsic motivations for learning," the university said.

Michigan is now the latest in a small group of schools throughout the country that have chosen to enact similar policies, including Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College and the California Institute of Technology.

CALIFORNIA PROFESSOR ARGUES NEED FOR 'OBJECTIVE MEASURES' AFTER STATE DROPS ACT/SAT REQUIREMENT

While the program is aimed at supporting students’ mental health, psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert believes it runs the risk of doing more harm than good.

"We’re raising a generation of students to believe that discomfort is dangerous," Alpert, author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital. "It isn’t. A bad grade can be upsetting, embarrassing and stressful. That’s not a mental health emergency. That’s college."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Alpert went on to add that while the policy was created to relieve students of the pressure and stress from the first semester of college, it could actually risk harming their preparedness for life outside of the learning environment.

"This is therapy culture invading the classroom. We’ve spent years turning normal human emotions into symptoms. Stress becomes a mental health issue," Alpert said, adding, "College should be one of the places where young people discover that they’re tougher than they think."

"A bad grade isn't psychological harm," Alpert continued. "Sometimes it's the wake-up call a student needs."

Fox News Digital reached out to the University of Michigan for comment.

item.title: Tori Spelling poses in racy bikini top as she addresses Jennie Garth podcast departure
item.description: Tori Spelling shared a bikini photo after confirming her departure from the "Beverly Hills, 90210" rewatch podcast with Jennie Garth.
item.content:encoded:
Tori Spelling is taking an "intermission" while navigating a new chapter in her life and career.

The 53-year-old actress shared a new photo of herself posing outdoors in a black halter-style bikini top and oversized denim shorts.

The "90210" alum accessorized with layered gold necklaces, oversized black sunglasses and green sandals as she stood on a sunlit wooden deck surrounded by trees and distant hills.

"Intermission," she captioned the post.

TORI SPELLING LIVING IN A 'BORDERLINE HOARDER' HOME AS LIVING CONDITIONS WORSEN

The brief message comes as Spelling steps away from one of the projects that kept her closely connected to her "Beverly Hills, 90210" past.

Spelling recently confirmed that she is no longer participating in "90210MG," the rewatch podcast she launched with former co-star Jennie Garth in 2020.

The "90210MG" podcast launched in November 2020, with Spelling and Garth revisiting "Beverly Hills, 90210" from the beginning and sharing memories from their years on the hit teen drama.

The rewatch has taken listeners back to West Beverly High, the Peach Pit and other memorable moments from the series while offering behind-the-scenes stories from the cast.

Nearly six years after its launch, the podcast is currently working its way through Season 8 of the show's 10-season run. Spelling's departure means she will not continue alongside Garth for the final stretch of the rewatch.

Spelling addressed her departure more directly during a recent episode of Brian Austin Green's "Hump Day Live," a weekly video series that streams on the Origami Network.

When Green suggested she needed "a little time" to gather her thoughts about the situation, Spelling agreed.

"I like the way you phrased that," she said. "Yeah. You want to really take the time, really assess, really reflect and then be able to speak your truth in a thoughtful way instead of a reactive way."

Green noted that he tries to avoid ruling anything out permanently, while Spelling did not directly say whether she could eventually return to the podcast.

Instead, she encouraged fans to continue supporting Garth and co-host Amy Sugarman.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Please, please, please keep watching," Spelling said. "Jennie and Amy [Sugarman] are doing it. They’re bringing on tons of fun hosts, so please keep watching it."

The exchange also highlighted Spelling’s enduring friendship with Green, who played her on-screen love interest David Silver opposite her Donna Martin on "Beverly Hills, 90210."

The two recently reunited for what Spelling called a "Play date," sharing photos together on Instagram and prompting nostalgic reactions from fans.

"David and Donna together again.💕 so awesome that you two have remained friends all these years," one commenter wrote.

Spelling has also been openly affectionate about her decades-long bond with Green.

For his birthday in July, she shared a tribute reflecting on how their friendship has evolved since their days working together on the hit series.

"He’s a little bit VINYL… I’m a little bit THREAD 🎵💃🏼. Happy Birthday @brianaustingreen," Spelling wrote.

"What a dream it’s been to grow with you. I’d choose you every lifetime. I love you with every ounce of my being. Don’t ever stop pushing me to be the best version of myself and I promise to never stop making you laugh! xo"

Spelling and Green's bond stretches back to their teenage years on "Beverly Hills, 90210," where they spent a decade playing fan-favorite couple Donna and David. Their relationship wasn't limited to the screen, with the co-stars becoming romantically involved early in the show's run.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Their lives eventually moved in different directions, and the two went years without communicating after the series ended. They have since found their way back to a close friendship, with Green now among the people Spelling has turned to while navigating changes in her personal and professional life.

Spelling’s decision to leave "90210MG" came with two seasons remaining in the podcast’s effort to rewatch all 10 seasons of the original series.

Garth addressed Spelling’s departure during the July 31 episode of "90210MG," admitting she was disappointed they wouldn't complete the rewatch together.

"I’m sad that she’s not finishing this out with us. We started this together. I’m sad about that, if I’m honest," Garth said.

However, she also expressed support for her former co-star’s decision.

TORI SPELLING SETS THE RECORD STRAIGHT ON 30 YEARS OF PLASTIC SURGERY RUMORS

"I’m really happy for her," Garth said. "I’m excited for her to choose herself."

Sugarman said Spelling’s departure was her own decision.

"This was 100 percent her decision," she said.

She added that the team could be disappointed by Spelling’s departure while still supporting whatever comes next.

"We can be really bummed, disappointed that she’s not going to do seasons 9 and 10 with us, with you, while still wanting her to be happy and to be excited for her about the things she is working on and does want to do," Sugarman said.

Spelling has not yet shared the full reason behind her exit, making clear that she wants time to process the decision before saying more.

item.title: Four criminally underrated guitarists from the 1980s that are guaranteed to melt your face off
item.description: From Reb Beach's legato runs in Winger to George Lynch's Sunset Strip shredding in Dokken, these '80s metal guitarists deserve far more recognition.
item.content:encoded:
This opinion might land me in some hot water with music purists everywhere, but I believe the greatest era of guitar wizardry came in the 1980s.

The decade featured some of the most revered and celebrated virtuosos to ever walk the planet, both critically and commercially.

But for every Eddie Van Halen or Randy Rhoads, there were plenty of other face-melters who existed in some form of relative obscurity compared to their more famous counterparts.

BARRY MANILOW RESCHEDULES CONCERT 45 MINUTES BEFORE START AMID ONGOING LUNG CANCER RECOVERY

That's not to say the bands these guitarists were in weren't successful in their own right, but if you were to ask a mainstream pop-listener from the era who these guys were, chances are you'd get looks of befuddlement.

Which is a shame, because these guys were just as talented (if not more talented) than some of the more popular axe-slingers of the 80s.

And hey, since I love you dear readers so much, I decided to include a bonus guest pick from my good buddy and fellow guitar junkie, Matt Reigle!

With that said, here are four (plus one) of the most criminally underrated guitarists from the Decade of Decadence.

Of all the late 80s hair metal groups who got unfairly characterized as a bunch of no-talent hacks, Winger might be the most egregious victim.

It's a fairly famous story by now, but some combination of Beavis and Butt-head roasting their nerdy friend for wearing a Winger shirt and Metallica drummer Lars Ulrich throwing darts at a picture of the hair band's frontman Kip Winger effectively ruined any credibility the band had.

Which is a shame, because, with all due respect to the members of Metallica, whom I have a great deal of respect for, the members of Winger could play circles around them.

Chief among those talented members is guitarist Reb Beach, whose buttery smooth legato tapping runs and percussive riffs like the one from hit-single "Seventeen" made him an underground guitar god in his own right.

Unfortunately, Winger committed the mortal sins of having a pretty boy lead singer and painfully cheesy videos (even by 80s standards), so most people dismissed them and Beach as cheap imitators.

Though his time in the spotlight was brief, any of guitar-oriented hair metal knows Beach is one of the more technically accomplished shredders of his era, Mike Judge be damned.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Their eponymous debut features some tasty licks and haunting solos and should be an immediate listen for any fans of the genre.

Metal acts from far off lands was nothing new even back in the mid-80s, as fellow Axis Power Germany showed us with groups like Accept and, more importantly, Scorpions, but Japan's Loudness filled the void of bands who melted face from the Land of the Rising Sun.

The group featured a singer who barely spoke a lick of English, so if you were looking for a hair metal act with poetic, introspective lyrics, you might want to search elsewhere (or pick a different genre entirely).

What they lacked in lyrical depth they made up for with crushing riffs and explosive solos courtesy of their fleet-fingered lead guitarist and founding member Akira Takasaki.

The first time I heard Loudness was on Satellite Radio driving back to college one weekend. The song in question was perhaps their most well-known, "Crazy Nights," off their 1985 glam metal masterpiece "Thunder in the East."

I was blown away by the balls on display from Takasaki's guitar tone and immediately went home and looked the band up only to be shocked to find out they hailed from Japan.

Takasaki's incendiary lead stylings and creative riffing likely inspired a million bedroom guitar players in Japan alone, and he has definitely influenced my tastes over the years as well.

The Sunset Strip is famous for producing hundreds of wildly talented shredders in the late 70s and early 80s, with the aforementioned Eddie Van Halen likely taking the crown as the king of Los Angeles-area guitarists from that era.

One six-stringed genius who came up right alongside Eddie was none other than George Lynch, lead guitarist extraordinaire from the hair metal band Dokken.

Dokken had everything you could want in a popular metal act in the early-to-mid 80s: a charismatic frontman, an untouchable lead guitar player, memorable songs, and catchy riffs.

The only problem is that the two principal members, Lynch and lead singer Don Dokken, absolutely despised each other, and that friction led to the band imploding right before their rocket went from "popular" to "superstars."

Despite this, Dokken released plenty of material beloved by both guitar tech-heads and leg warmer-wearing chicks of the 80s, and Lynch etched out a spot in metal history with his blistering solo runs and deceptively heavy hooks.

Mr. Scary himself is often seen as the third head in the Sunset Strip triumvirate of himself, Van Halen and Rhoads, and anyone worth their salt in the guitar community has absolutely counted him as an influence in their playing.

I know I've invoked his name quite a bit throughout this article, but Eddie Van Halen is my favorite guitarist of all-time.

He has been the most influential on my personal style of playing by far and his band is my number one by a country mile.

With all that being said, many people may be surprised to learn that my second-favorite axe-slinger is none other than Ratt's Warren DeMartini.

The guy had it all: rip-roaring solos, creative and catchy riffs, and a cool, calm, and collected demeanor that had many tabbing him as the 1980s' answer to Joe Perry.

DeMartini was a principal songwriter on two of Ratt's biggest hits, "Round and Round" and "Lay It Down," showing that he had a knack for crafting radio-friendly tunes just as much as he had a mastery of the fretboard.

Ratt had lasting popular appeal throughout the 80s, but it was always a case of the sum being more notorious than its parts, so DeMartini never got the acclaim he rightly deserved.

Their first three full-length albums, "Out of the Cellar," "Invasion of Your Privacy" and "Dancing Undercover," represent some of the finest pop-metal the era had to offer, and several students of the 80s guitar scene will often cite these as quasi-sacred texts from which they pull inspiration quite often.

There are plenty of guitar heroes in the Big 4 thrash metal bands like James Hetfield, Kirk Hammett, Kerry King, Jeff Hanneman, Dave Mustaine, Marty Friedman and Scott Ian.

But while Ian gets most of the attention in Anthrax due to him being the band leader and a monster rhythm player, someone had to play the leads on the band’s biggest songs like "Caught in a Mosh," "Indians" and "Madhouse."

That was Dan Spitz.

Spitz played on every Anthrax album from their debut, "Fistful of Metal," to 1993’s "Sound of White Noise."

He briefly reunited with the band in the mid-aughts, but I think he gets overlooked because he wasn’t in the band for the re-appreciation of classic thrash that came about through the 2010s.

Spitz brought some unique flavor to Anthrax.

His leads and contributions to the band’s famous forays into rap metal are huge. He was responsible for the short acoustic piece, "A.D.I.," which serves as the intro to the song "Horror of it All."

It’s a real change-up on the album with some really solid, Middle Eastern-inspired playing.

But I think the high-water mark is his lead on the song "Only" from "Sound of White Noise."

It’s an absolute monster solo that can rip your face off through the first two-thirds, then shifts gears into a section with some of the most deliciously wah-soaked melodic phrasing you’ll ever hear.

It’s so, so good.

item.title: Antonio Banderas says he always knew Los Angeles wasn't where he belonged
item.description: Antonio Banderas reveals why he left Los Angeles for Málaga after his divorce from Melanie Griffith, calling her one of his best friends today.
item.content:encoded:
Antonio Banderas is getting real about why he ditched Los Angeles to move back to his hometown in Spain.

During a recent interview with People, the 65-year-old explained he originally moved to Los Angeles to be with Melanie Griffith after the two fell in love. She had two young children at the time and couldn't relocate to Spain.

"Those were beautiful, exciting years. But I always had this sense of provisionality that it was not going to last my whole life," Banderas said. "I knew that Málaga was there, my hometown. I was not supposed to be in Malibu, but in Málaga."

Griffith and Banderas went on to marry in 1996, just one year after making a connection on set of the 1995 movie "Two Much." Not long after tying the knot, the two welcomed their daughter, Stella, in September 1996.

'FIRE COUNTRY' STAR DIANE FARR LEAVES LOS ANGELES AFTER 30 YEARS TO START HER 'THIRD ACT'

The two were married for 18 years before Griffith filed for divorce in June 2014, citing irreconcilable differences. They went on to finalize their divorce a little over a year later, in December 2015.

"When we separated, we were always very sincere. And now she is, if not my best friend, one of my best friends," Banderas explained.

While married to Griffith, Banderas was stepfather to her two children, Alexander Bauer and actress Dakota Johnson.

When speaking to E! News in February 2025, Banderas admitted he "would love to work with Dakota someday," not only because she is his family, but "because she's a good actress."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"She's a good actress in many different ways, because she's a great comedian, too," he said. "She developed now her career more in drama, but I remember when she did a TV show called Ben and Kate that I got a lot of fun [out of seeing] her on the screen, because she got the rhythm of comedy, too."

Banderas is currently starring in the Anthony Bourdain biopic "Tony," but got his big break in mainstream American films in the 1993 movie "Philadelphia."

He went on to star in "Interview with the Vampire," "Desperado," "The Mask of Zorro" and others, including "Pain and Glory" in 2020, which earned him an Academy Award nomination.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

During an interview with The Times in March, Banderas reflected on the early days of his career, and recalled being told upon his arrival in Hollywood that he was there "like the Blacks and the Hispanics, to play the bad guys."

"The problem was, a few years later, I had a mask, hat, sword and cape and the bad guy was Captain Love, who was blond and had blue eyes," he said. "Even more important is 'Puss in Boots,' because it's for young kids. They see a cat that has a Spanish, even an Andalusian accent, and he's a good guy."

item.title: Maher blasts Rand Paul for releasing Fauci’s COVID diaries as PR expert suggests a new course for the Senator
item.description: Comedian Bill Maher accused Rand Paul of betraying his libertarian brand by releasing Fauci's private COVID-19 diary and pursuing contempt charges.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Bill Maher is taking aim at Sen. Rand Paul for what the host says betrays Paul's own brand.

During Friday's episode of HBO's "Real Time," Maher accused Paul, R-Ky., of breaking with his libertarian views by releasing Fauci's pandemic-era diary and threatening to hold him in contempt of Congress. Meanwhile, a public relations expert told Fox News Digital that Paul should focus on why the diary matters rather than how he obtained it.

"Stop threatening to put everyone in jail who you just don’t like," Maher said more broadly about politics. 

"Rand, babe, your entire brand is ‘Senator Right to Privacy,’" he added. "You’re the libertarian guy, the Fourth Amendment guy. It’s your family legacy."

BILL MAHER BREAKS WITH THE LEFT TO HAMMER ANTHONY FAUCI AFTER EXPLOSIVE SENATE HEARING

Maher’s comments come on the heels of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which is led by Paul, voting 8-5 to refer Fauci for contempt after he repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment during a Senate hearing regarding his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic last week.

Fauci, who received a preemptive pardon from then-President Joe Biden last year, exercised his right against self-incrimination a total of 111 times during the hearing while being questioned over his leadership as the White House chief medical adviser during the pandemic.

In the days before the hearing, Paul released more than 1000 pages of Fauci's private "COVID diaries" — medical notes and personal reflections Fauci wrote and stored on his government computer.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

The move was blasted by Maher, who argued Paul's decision to publish the documents directly contradicted his longtime political platform of personal privacy and limited government intrusion.

"Your entire political career has been about warning us about government overreach," Maher said, speaking directly to Paul. "You printing someone's diary? It's like [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] wearing a gown that says, ‘Tax the poor.’"

Fauci's diaries were located and stored on government servers. 

Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, told Fox News Digital that the criticism surrounding Paul's release of Fauci's private diary is unfounded, while adding he would advise Paul to change approach to explaining why the document is important.

"If Sen. Paul were my client, I’d tell him to stop defending how he got the diary and start defending why it matters," Mudd said. "A public official’s notes on a government computer aren’t a private citizen’s journal, and that distinction should have been his first sentence, not his fifth."  

Maher’s comments come after he previously made headlines by suggesting that his "vote is in play" after voicing his discontent with the socialist direction the Democratic party is heading.

"Politically, Bill Maher carries resonance with a fairly non-tribal group of viewers. While that means he can often piss off both sides, it also means he can be seen as above the partisan back-and-forth, without a specific left or right agenda," media expert Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital.

DAVID MARCUS: BILL MAHER'S NO REPUBLICAN, HE'S JUST A RARE DEMOCRAT WHO THINKS

Shroff added that Maher's words carry more weight when he criticizes both sides of the political spectrum because of his willingness to call out his own party.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Maher can spend one week arguing that Democrats have lost the plot and the next saying Republicans have gone too far," Shroff said. "That gives moments like this outsized significance: when someone who has repeatedly criticized Fauci and the left still looks at what Rand Paul is doing and says it crosses a line, it gives permission to viewers who aren’t particularly sympathetic to Fauci to reach the same conclusion."

"In a polarized media environment, the messenger can matter as much as the message," Shroff added.

item.title: Joe Biden's cancer has spread further, leaving him in 'very painful' condition, Hunter reveals

item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him significant pain, his son Hunter Biden revealed during a Friday interview.

"The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," Hunter Biden told the BBC in an interview which aired Friday. "It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects," he added.

"It’s really sad to watch," Hunter Biden said. "The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good."

HUNTER BIDEN CLAIMS UNDER OATH THAT HIS FAMILY IS BROKE AMID FIGHT OVER $17M LEGAL BILL

"He had it while he was president," said Dr. Ezekiel J. Emanuel, vice provost and oncologist at the University of Pennsylvania, adding Joe Biden "probably had it at the start of his presidency in 2021."

item.title: Florida business owners allegedly scattered 1,500 mothballs on beach to send endangered birds packing
item.description: Two St. Pete Beach business owners allegedly spread 1,500 toxic mothballs on sand to stop black skimmers from nesting, now facing felony charges.
item.content:encoded:
Two Florida business owners have been charged with third-degree felonies after allegedly spreading about 1,500 "toxic" mothballs across a beach in hopes of keeping an "imperiled" bird species from nesting there.

If convicted, they could each face up to five years in prison, fines of up to $5,000 and up to five years of probation.

The problem started in late April when beachgoers noticed mothballs on the white, sugary sand on St. Pete Beach in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and bird-loving volunteers from the Audubon Society mobilized. They plucked about 1,000 of the small, white orbs from the sand behind the Plaza Beach Hotel.

MASSACHUSETTS HOMEOWNERS STUNNED AFTER TOWN WARNS JULY 4 FLAGS THREATEN ENDANGERED BIRDS

Then 500 more appeared overnight.

The smelly balls containing pesticides dotted an area where endangered shorebirds known as black skimmers were "attempting to establish a nesting colony," FWC officials said in a news conference. Their placement also meant other wildlife and children "could easily come in contact with them."

It quickly became clear that someone might be targeting the birds, they said.

So FWC investigators flew into action.

Meanwhile, the discovery of the mothballs ruffled feathers in the community.

There was "a lot of public outcry" expressing concern for the birds, while investigators tried to locate the source of the mothballs, FWC officials said.

Law enforcement served search warrants, combed through "terabytes" of data and eventually seized cellphones to try to locate the individuals behind the caper.

That work led them to Christopher Monroe, owner and manager of Chris’s Beachside Bar, and Robert Czyszczon, owner of the Plaza Beach Hotel, FWC officials said.

Out of fear of lost revenue, the two allegedly hatched a plan to use mothballs to deter birds from congregating on the beach behind their businesses, authorities said.

HIKERS FACE $25,000 FINE AFTER OFF-LEASH DOG BARKED AT GRIZZLY BEAR ON BANFF NATIONAL PARK TRAIL

Through video surveillance and receipt records, investigators found that Czyszczon spent about $60 buying "a large quantity" of mothballs at a Walmart the day before they first appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

Upon examining his phone, investigators found "incriminating" text messages between him and fellow business owner, Monroe, discussing their objections to the native fowl.

Text conversations revealed plans for placement of the mothballs on the beach, officials said. That’s what led investigators to Monroe as a suspect.

The men discussed how they "were going to do something" to prevent the birds from nesting on the beach, FWC officials said.

Black skimmers don’t nest in trees. They kick beach sand backwards to make depressions on the ground. Then they lay their eggs and raise their young near the surf.

"They're the worst birds," one of the men allegedly wrote in anticipation of nesting season.

"The bird people will put up fence around the area, and then the beach people will not be able to get to and from because they will fence around that space."

Cellphone tower data showed Monroe’s phone was at the same location as Czyszczon’s phone on both nights when the mothballs appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

The men feared that nests on the beach would lead to fewer customers and less money being spent there, authorities said.

"Why didn't you tell me we lose $25,000 to $50,000?" one allegedly wrote in a text.

Monroe and Czyszczon were charged with illegal dumping, a third-degree felony, according to Pinellas County court records. They also were charged with the "attempted take of a state-listed imperiled species by harassment," a misdemeanor, according to FWC officials.

Both are out of jail on bond.

MASSACHUSETTS HOMEOWNERS STUNNED AFTER TOWN WARNS JULY 4 FLAGS THREATEN ENDANGERED BIRDS

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

About 6,800 black skimmers live in Florida. FWC officials estimate that several hundred live on the beaches of Pinellas County.

SEND US A TIP

The pesticide in mothballs can harm people and wildlife that come into contact with their vapors, according to an educational publication by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (IFAS).

"With any pesticide, the label is the law," Brett W. Bultemeier, director of the UF/IFAS Pesticide Information Office, wrote in a 2021 educational publication about mothballs. "The label language is not simply a set of directions. Rather, they are requirements that are legally enforceable."

GOT A TIP?

The birds probably weren’t hurt by the "harassment," FWC officials said.

But it did delay their nesting, they said. That pushes the date that their young can fledge from the nest further back in the season. And that could put them in danger.

A big storm at the end of hurricane season, which ends on Nov. 30, "can wipe out a colony if those young birds haven't fledged yet," an FWC official said.

An attorney for Czyszczon did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. Court records indicate that Monroe doesn’t have an attorney. He couldn’t be reached for comment.

item.title: Cornell bans bear butchering after students carved up creature in dorm kitchen
item.description: Cornell University now bans wild game processing in dorm kitchens after two students went viral for butchering a black bear in Ganędagǫ Hall.
item.content:encoded:
Cornell University has added a new rule banning the processing of wild game in school kitchens months after two students went viral for carving up a bear in a dormitory kitchen.

"Processing wild/game animals in community kitchens is strictly prohibited," the school's new policy reads.

The school confirmed to a student newspaper that the rule's addition was a direct response to the 2025 incident, which saw two students drag the carcass of a black bear they had killed into Cornell's Ganędagǫ Hall for preparation.

One of those students, Aaron Chin, revealed himself as one of the butchers on a podcast a few months after the incident.

CODY JOHNSON FIRES BACK AT CRITICS, CALLS ALASKA GRIZZLY BEAR HUNT A 'CONSERVATIONIST EFFORT'

Chin explained that he and his hunting partner, a fellow Cornell student, had planned on bringing the bear from the hunting grounds located roughly two hours from the school to a friend's house to prepare it, but claimed the friend had an emergency that left them unable to use his home.

Chin also said that before bringing the bear meat on campus, he and his partner ensured they weren't breaking any campus rules.

"We were really diligent in reading all of the rules [and] regulations," Chin told the MeatEater podcast in September. "We made sure we did everything by the book because we knew we were going to be under scrutiny."

The incident incurred swift social media and on-campus backlash, prompting state regulators to investigate.

However, after an inspector from New York's Department of Environmental Conservation visited the kitchen where the carving took place, the agency found no code violations, according to an NBC report.

item.title: White Sox manager Will Venable forgets key rule in inexplicable blunder, costs team in loss
item.description: Will Venable forgot a key mound visit rule, forcing Noah Schultz out after just five batters and taxing an already exhausted Chicago White Sox bullpen.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable has done a tremendous job in his first season with the club, with many fine moments throughout the season.

However, in the White Sox’s 8-2 loss to the Cleveland Guardians at Rate Field on Friday, Venable did not have one of his finer moments, as he forgot a key rule and cost his team dearly.

Just four batters into the game, White Sox starting pitcher Noah Schultz had loaded the bases, drawing a mound visit from pitching coach Zach Bove. One batter later, left fielder Angel Martinez ripped a two-run single.

Venable then went to the mound to talk about an appeal play but forgot that he wasn’t allowed to do so.

Under official rule 5.10(l), "a manager or coach is allowed only one visit to the mound per pitcher in a single inning without penalty. If the same coach or manager makes a second visit to the same pitcher in the same inning, the pitcher must be removed from the pitching position."

Venable’s visit to the mound meant that he had to remove Schultz from the game just five batters in. His gaffe was especially costly, because the team lost in 13 innings the night before and taxed its bullpen.

Venable’s blunder meant that his already taxed bullpen was going to have to work 8 2/3 innings. David Sandlin, who replaced Schultz, hadn’t even begun throwing in the bullpen when Venable went to the pitcher’s mound; he was just getting loose and stretching.

"Yeah, just an inexcusable mistake by me where we had an appeal play that we wanted to execute, and in the urgency of trying to make that happen, just totally lost that we had visited," Venable said, according to MLB.com. "Obviously that was a mistake. So, just messed it up."

item.title: Jamie Kennedy blasts left-wing double standards following 'maggot' attacks
item.description: Jamie Kennedy says he's labeled a "maggot" for supporting Trump policies and slams the left as fake on inclusion during a fiery podcast episode.
item.content:encoded:
Jamie Kennedy is calling out what he sees as hypocrisy in America today.

The actor released a solo episode of his podcast, "Hate to Break It to Ya," this week, and spoke at length about current events, namely the Fauci hearings and the renewed conversation around the COVID-19 pandemic and its lasting effects.

During the episode, Kennedy's discussion of the public response to the pandemic became a bit broader when he spoke about some people today being "beyond brainwashed."

JAMIE KENNEDY BLASTS MARK HAMILL'S DEAD TRUMP POST AS 'EVIL' AFTER ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT

"And I've never seen this in the history of our race of human beings," he continued. "For instance, if I like something that a Republican does, or Trump does, they call me not just MAGA, they call me a maggot. A maggot."

He explained that while he does lean right, he "never even voted," and he said there are some more liberal policies he agrees with as well, "but if I say I like that Trump secures the borders, I'm just a maggot."

The "Scream" star said he believes that people like him, who focus on policy over party, are "open-minded," while people on the left have "no leniency."

"How can you say that you're the party of inclusion when you don't include us?" he asked. "All we want to do is talk to people, figure out things, go through different ideas, see what we like. And if we don't, we don't feel like we've looked under every stone. And I feel like that's what's happening – people don't want you to investigate. If you even investigate or go against their beliefs, they just put you in a box."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Kennedy also spoke about performing an hour-long comedy set in a parking lot to raise money for a bar that had been struggling to stay afloat under lockdown restrictions. The event was nearly shut down while, at the same time, he claimed, a crew of dozens was shooting a television show in another parking lot nearby with no issues because it had been "sanctioned by the state."

item.title: Couples asking wedding guests for cash spark fierce debate over manners and tradition
item.description: AnnaLynne McCord and Danny Cipriani's Honeyfund wedding registry sparks a heated debate over whether asking guests for cash is tacky or modern.
item.content:encoded:
A request by a celebrity couple that their wedding guests help fund their nuptials is being branded "tacky" by some — while others insist cash is king.

American actress AnnaLynne McCord, known for her roles on "90210," "Nip/Tuck" and "Days of Our Lives," and her English former professional rugby player fiancé, Danny Cipriani, set up a page on Honeyfund, an online wedding and honeymoon registry, inviting people to contribute to wish-list elements of their "dream wedding."

The registry lists wedding expenses ranging from $100 to $600, including the marriage license, reception beverages, photography, rehearsal dinner and floral arrangements.

COURTHOUSE WEDDINGS ARE BOOMING AS MANY COUPLES SKIP PRICEY TRADITIONAL CEREMONIES

"Tacky is an ugly word, but it’s really unkind to ask your guests to give you money for any occasion," Texas-based etiquette expert Diane Gottsman told Fox News Digital. "It really is impolite to straight out ask for cash. You let your family do the talking for you. You let your website do the talking for you."

Gottsman said every couple needs a wedding registry to give options for guests, but asking directly for cash sets the wrong tone immediately.

Cash is easy to give, she added, and is acceptable to include as a request on a website for honeymoon funds, a down payment for a home, etc. — but it shouldn’t be the only option. Some guests prefer to give a gift, and it should be left up to them.

"A gift is not an admission ticket to your wedding," Gottsman said. "A registry makes it easier, but guests can do whatever they would like. It’s a gracious act of giving that they’re doing for you."

Several Reddit discussions about cash wedding registries suggest attitudes vary, with some users saying the practice is a modern, accepted trend. Gottsman clarified that a cash option is perfectly acceptable, but that asking guests to pay for the wedding itself is "off-putting."

One Reddit forum asked, "Is it bad to ask for money instead of gifts?"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"No, most people do this now — majority of [the] weddings I’ve been to the last few years all were mainly cash registries," one user replied.

"We did, and didn’t get any backlash and got money from everyone, except one friend who offered us either money or getting a meat subscription box," another user responded. "And we love to cook, and good meat is dang expensive, so we took it — but we didn’t get any surprise gifts from people who refused to give us cash or anything like that."

A Redditor identifying as an Asian person said the only gift you give or receive in that culture is money.

"Can someone please explain to me why it is such a ‘bad’ thing to not have a physical registry? Like, I don’t get it," the person wrote. "If I want something, you giving me the money will let me buy it. If I already have everything I need, money can help re-coop the cost of the wedding or literally anything else. Money is the best, most versatile gift."

"Why in American culture is it seen so negatively?" the person added. "I’m born and raised in the U.S., and I still never understood people’s issue with this."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"It’s a general taboo around money in American culture," a fellow Redditor replied. "You’re not supposed to talk about money at all, honestly. So asking for it or exchanging it directly is frowned upon. That’s why there’s such a culture around signaling wealth indirectly. Having a big wedding or designer bags is how to flaunt wealth, not posting a screenshot of your bank statement."

Someone else on Reddit asked if it would be rude to ask for money instead of gifts for her wedding — then edited the original post to say she decided against it and to include cash as an option among other gifts on her registry.

"Just have a honeymoon fund and few or no physical items on your registry, and most people will take the hint," someone on the forum advised.

Gottsman encouraged couples to "think about the ask." 

They should throw a wedding they can afford, because asking for cash sets a different tone for the celebration.

If a guest is reluctant to chip in on a couple’s wedding, Gottsman said there’s a gracious way to decline.

"Say, ‘I have something else in mind, and I’m really hoping you enjoy it,’ not, ‘I’m not giving you cash, because it annoys me,’" she said.

A timeless, go-to gift for a couple is something sentimental and thoughtful that you know the couple will like.

If you don’t have any ideas, give them something they can return. 

Make sure you are always including a gift receipt, Gottsman said.

item.title: Hawaii voters hit the polls as Gov. Josh Green dominates, progressive takes aim at Dem congressman
item.description: Hawaii's 1st Congressional District primary pits Rep. Ed Case against Jarrett Keohokalole, who opposes Donald Trump tariffs and ICE enforcement.
item.content:encoded:
Hawaii voters will decide Saturday who advances to the November general election, with key contests including the race for governor and the battle to represent the state’s 1st Congressional District.

Gov. Josh Green, who was first elected in 2022, is heavily favored to win the Democratic primary, where he faces three little-known competitors. His challengers include George "Teva" Lucas-Tadeo, a Democratic socialist who has promised on social media to open a government-run grocery store and legalize recreational marijuana.

David "Duke" Bourgoin is mounting his second primary challenge against Green after losing to him in 2022, when he captured only 590 votes against Green’s 158,161. He also lost two bids for Honolulu mayor, in 2022 and 2024.

JOHNSON'S STRATEGY TO BYPASS DEMOCRATS' SAVE ACT BLOCKADE SURVIVES KEY VOTE, HANDING GOP BIG WIN

Lauren Kapoliahiʻiaka Shim is also seeking the Democratic nomination. She is the CEO and founder of Aloha AI Incorporated, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Neither Lucas-Tadeo nor Shim had campaign websites, and none of Green’s three challengers had raised any money in the race as of June 30, according to Honolulu Civil Beat. Meanwhile, Green has raised approximately $3.5 million, far outpacing Republican Gary Cordery, the race’s second-highest fundraiser, who has raised about $313,000, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.

Cordery, owner of the contracting company Kingdom Builders, and Ken Fujiyama, an entrepreneur and investor, are competing for the Republican nomination and a chance to end nearly two decades of Democratic control of the governor’s mansion. The last Republican to serve as Hawaii governor was Linda Lingle, who held the office from 2002 to 2010.

Cordery has campaigned on lowering Hawaii’s high cost of living, expanding housing and cracking down on government waste and corruption. He has proposed adding 15,000 homes for working families, using state-owned land for housing and eliminating the state’s general excise tax on food and medicine. Fujiyama has also proposed a plan to tackle the housing affordability crisis by developing 100,000 residential lots and partnering with large landowners to spur growth.

MICHIGAN’S TOP ELECTION OFFICIAL WINS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR, ADVANCES TO BATTLEGROUND RACE

Whoever emerges from the Republican primary will face an uphill battle to unseat Green if he secures the Democratic nomination. Green holds a 56% approval rating, while the Cook Political Report rates the race "Likely Democrat" and gives Democrats a 13-point advantage.

Meanwhile, eyes outside of Hawaii will be locked on the Democratic primary in the 1st Congressional District, where state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole is challenging Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii.

Case, who is seeking a seventh term, has represented the district since 2019 and argues that his seniority and position on the Appropriations Committee give Hawaii greater influence in Washington. Meanwhile, Keohokalole, who is endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders' group Our Revolution, is running on a progressive platform that includes Medicare for All and opposition to ICE and President Donald Trump's tariffs.

Keohokalole is seeking to portray Case as out of touch with Democratic voters, pointing to the congressman’s vote with House Republicans to pass Trump's SAVE America Act, which would require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

Given the district’s strong Democratic lean, whoever wins the party’s primary will likely be favored to win the seat in November.

Polls close at 7pm local time.

item.title: 'Remember the Titans' star Ethan Suplee says one hard truth fueled his 300-pound weight loss
item.description: Ethan Suplee reveals how treating weight loss like his sobriety helped him maintain a 300-pound transformation after years of failed attempts.
item.content:encoded:
"Remember the Titans" star Ethan Suplee spent years dramatically transforming his body, but the actor says the breakthrough that finally helped him maintain his weight loss came when he stopped viewing it as something he could permanently "cure."

Suplee explained he saw the biggest change when he began treating his relationship with food and weight much like his sobriety — a lifelong condition requiring honesty, communication and accountability.

Reflecting on his recovery journey with Fox News Digital, Suplee said repeated attempts to get sober failed because he believed he could simply complete rehab and move on. He believed taking 30 days away from drugs and alcohol meant the problem had gone away.

"I haven’t had drugs or alcohol in 30 days," he recalled. "That means I’m cured."

'REMEMBER THE TITANS' STAR ETHAN SUPLEE ISSUES WARNING ABOUT WEIGHT LOSS DRUG CRAZE

It wasn't until he embraced ongoing accountability and open communication that he found lasting success, a lesson he later realized applied just as much to maintaining his weight loss.

"My condition isn’t a condition with a cure," Suplee explained. "It’s a condition that I can learn to manage."

He added, "I did not apply that to weight loss for many, many years. I kind of was doing everything in my head, and the big boon to actually being able to maintain it was finding a group of people to be accountable to."

CELEBRITY CHEF REVEALS NO. 1 MISTAKE SABOTAGING YOUR WEIGHT LOSS: 'FUZZY MATH'

Suplee has been candid about his decades-long battle with obesity. The "My Name is Earl" actor weighed roughly 500 pounds at his heaviest and ultimately lost around 300 pounds through years of diet and lifestyle changes. He has also undergone multiple skin-removal surgeries and now hosts weekly discussions on his show, "LifeLONG with Ethan Suplee," about long-term weight management.

"There’s some pressure from the world to continue to manage [the weight loss]," he told Fox News Digital. "But that’s something I’ve kind of designed."

On his weekly live show and podcast, "LifeLONG," Suplee regularly discusses the realities of long-term weight maintenance, inviting experts and people who have transformed their health to talk about nutrition, emotional eating, fitness and accountability. The show's central message is that health is an ongoing practice — not a destination.

"It’s a group of people, like-minded people, who come in, and we share what we’re going through, and we share our experience," Suplee explained. "And I think we all do better because of that."

After decades of trial and error, Suplee said his own experience taught him there is no shortcut to lasting weight loss. While he acknowledged that weight-loss drugs can be an effective tool, he argued they aren't a replacement for building healthier habits.

"As a kid, I wanted a magical diet drug so badly. And now we have what is a magical diet drug," he said. "I think, unfortunately, it's also not a one-stop shop. I think you can hop on a GLP-1 and experience weight loss. You can see the scale go down week over week for a long time without having to do anything else."

"... I think when people imagine their ideal – I don't think the GLP-1s get anyone to their ideal."

Suplee said his own experience ultimately shaped a simple philosophy: There's no single answer when it comes to long-term weight loss.

He emphasized that lasting success comes from addressing the many factors that influence a person's health and relationship with food.

"I don't think it's ever going to be one thing," Suplee explained. "I think it is partially the amount of food you're consuming, partially the types of food you're consuming, partially how sedentary you are, and partially your emotional and potentially mental behavior and relationship with food."

item.title: Charles Barkley dunks all over pickleball: 'All these old people are killing themselves'
item.description: Charles Barkley calls pickleball 'the gift that keeps giving' for doctors, warning George Kittle about sports injuries plaguing older players.
item.content:encoded:
Former NBA legend Charles Barkley is certainly a very opinionated man, and when he has an opinion, he isn't afraid to let it fly.

The man who once famously said "I am not a role model" joined "The Kittle Cast" with NFL tight end George Kittle and his wife, Claire, and was giving out some rather sage advice about aging athletically.

For guys like Kittle and Barkley, going from the top of your game to retirement can be rough; it can feel like there's a hole in your life where your passion used to be.

That's why Sir Charles felt it paramount to impart his wisdom onto the younger Kittle now so he knows what to expect when he does decide to hang it up.

For Chuck, there is a list of dos and don'ts when it comes to staying in shape post-retirement, and while sharing this with the podcast power couple, he decided to take a shot at a very popular sport among retirees.

"There’s not a lot you can do when you get old," Barkley said. "You can’t go play basketball.

"And let me tell you something. They got this stupid thing going around called pickleball, which is the way old people out here are getting hurt all the time."

So, the Round Mound of Rebound is not a big pickleball fan? Got it.

But he continues.

"My doctor friends said pickleball is the gift that keeps giving," Barkley claims. "Because all these old people are killing themselves and hurt all the time. My doctor friends are in heaven right now."

Kittle chimes in and says he's heard similar things about America's fastest-growing sport among the 55-and-over community, citing torn ACLs and broken wrists galore.

"I am never stepping on that damn court," Kittle exclaimed.

I have to say, as someone who was conscripted into the pickleball cult back in 2023 and having "left the reservation," I couldn't agree more.

I was 30 years old thinking this was going to be some relaxing way to spend my weekends as a recently married guy trying to find a hobby, and I could not have been more wrong.

The word "cutthroat" is an understatement.

I was going up against guys (and girls) who were playing this sport as if it was the fifth set of the Australian Open Finals, and the funniest part of all of it was that most of these people were my age or slightly younger.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Mamdani's faux African accent as telling as it is bizarre
item.description: A resurfaced 2016 video shows Zohran Mamdani speaking in a full African/South Asian accent while promoting a Disney film he worked on as a dance adviser.
item.content:encoded:
In a resurfaced 2016 interview, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks for the entire time in an African/South Asian accent that sounds like a mix between Trevor Noah and Apu from "The Simpsons." It is absolutely bizarre, but it is also telling.

At the time, he was promoting a Disney movie that he had worked on as a dance adviser, one of the few actual jobs hizzoner has ever held. His signature smile is on display, but when he opens his lips he sounds like someone we have never heard.

With his sing-songy affected voice he decries how in Africa everybody dances, but in New York the men "just grind," but don’t dance. It is a performance entirely in character, he even imitates some Bollywood-style dance moves.

FLASHBACK: MAMDANI'S HISTORY OF DODGING QUESTIONS ABOUT WHERE HE STANDS ON KEY ISSUES

This is not Hillary Clinton’s voice getting a bit twangly when she speaks in the South. This is a full-on acting job, and further proof that the theater kids have taken over the American Left.

There is nothing inherently wrong with theater kids. I myself plied the boards in New York for many years before my career in journalism. But I never did an entire interview with a fake accent as if it was how I actually spoke, and neither did anyone else I know.

Because that is simply downright bizarre behavior.

This is not the first time we have seen different versions of Mamdani that seem like entirely different people. We have also seen him furious and screaming while protesting against ICE in a way that is entirely antithetical to the calm, never flustered, smiley character he plays now, as mayor.

TOM HOMAN WARNS ICE SURGE COMING TO NEW YORK CITY AS MAMDANI BOASTS ABOUT SANCTUARY STATUS

Mamdani’s defenders say that he is merely "code-switching," and that so-called marginalized people will subconsciously speak one way with their own group and another way outside of it. Sorry, but this accent was so perfected and performative that there is zero chance he didn’t know he was doing it.

It does raise an interesting question though: Is the African accent how Zany Zohran really talks, behind closed doors? Could it be his American accent that is the performance? We can’t really know.

In a way, this goofy accent incident is a good metaphor for Democratic Socialism writ large. For outside audiences, they speak in Americanized, vague terms about helping the working class, but you get these same people on a private Zoom call and it's blood and guts communism all the way down.

How many times have we heard "Oh, they aren’t really socialists, they are Democratic Socialists," as if there is one scintilla of difference once they start talking about abolishing the Senate, controlling the housing market and seizing the means of production?

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

One does have to admit, though, that the casting directors at the DSA hit the ball out of the park with Zohran. His fake plastic smile is the pitch-perfect mask for his Marxism. But who really lies underneath? The African choreographer? The furious protester? All of them?

The overwhelming sense one gets with these DSA candidates, like Mamdani, and Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and even Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, is that they are carefully curating just how radical they can appear to be to normal, everyday Americans, while their diehard supporters are in on the joke.

This was on display at El-Sayed’s victory party, last week, when he and podcasting antisemite Hasan Piker were talking to a supporter who told them, "People are stupid. This politics of no translation is going to be the way forward, money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all. No one has to decipher what that means." Piker and El-Sayed both appeared in agreement.

Mamdani and the DSA have proven that they will adopt any accent, don any garb, and utter any platitude to get the only thing that they really want, which is power over our lives.

The problem for New Yorkers and Americans is that we can have no idea what really lies beneath the many masks of Mamdani, whether he is the calm smiley American guy, the frothing lunatic protester, or the goofy African choreographer.

In fact, it seems like Mamdani is simply whoever he thinks you want him to be at any given moment. But it's getting old. As his budget numbers fail to line up and rents keep soaring, Gotham needs a leader, not a character actor.

Please, Mr. Mayor, we are all asking you, will the real Mamdani please stand up?
